SK5020 A cipher initialisation vector fixed at compile time

The initialisation vector is a constant, an array of zeros, or the key — so it is not a vector, it is a second constant.

CategorySecurity
Default severityerror
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS3329

Why

CBC exists to stop the thing ECB does: it chains each block into the next so that identical plaintext blocks encrypt differently. The chain has to start somewhere, and the initialisation vector is that start. If it is the same on every message, the chain begins identically every time — so two messages that share a prefix produce ciphertext that shares a prefix, and an observer learns that they are related and where they diverge, which is exactly the structure SK5005 reports ECB for leaking. It gets worse than leakage: with a predictable IV an attacker who can get a chosen plaintext encrypted can test guesses about an unknown block, which is the BEAST attack. The IV is not a secret and it is not a second key — it must be unpredictable, and it travels with the ciphertext in the clear. GenerateIV() draws a fresh one per message from the platform's cryptographic generator; prepend it to the output and read it back before decrypting. AesGcm takes a nonce and does the same job while also authenticating the ciphertext, so an attacker cannot flip bits in a message you will decrypt and act on. ⚠ There is no fix on the diagnostic, and that is the range's "rarely" column rather than a gap: making the IV fresh means also writing it into the message and reading it back at the other end, which changes the ciphertext format — every value already encrypted becomes unreadable by the new code. That is a migration, exactly as it is for SK5005.

Example

Instead of:

using var cipher = Aes.Create();
cipher.Key = key;
cipher.IV = new byte[16];
using var encryptor = cipher.CreateEncryptor();

Write:

using var cipher = Aes.Create();
cipher.Key = key;
cipher.GenerateIV();
await output.WriteAsync(cipher.IV);
using var encryptor = cipher.CreateEncryptor();

When it does not fire

⚠ The shape is hosted by `CA5401` and the host is not usable, which is why this is a rule rather than an entry in the hosted map. Measured on a plain net10.0 project built outside this repository with empty Directory.Build.props/.targets above it: CA5401 is off by default — analysislevelsecurity_10_default.globalconfig carries no rule entries at all, so a security CA's default is its own descriptor's — and once enabled it reports aes.IV = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(16) and aes.CreateEncryptor(key, RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(16)), both of which are the correct code. Its question is "is the IV non-default", and the answer is yes for every program that transmits an IV with its ciphertext. ⚠ The reason narrowing it is allowed here where doc 08 refused to narrow `CA5394` for #140 is that this narrowing needs no judgement: separating a security-sensitive Random from a statistical one means reading identifier names, which is what cut SK5008, whereas "is this expression a compile-time constant" is a fact the compiler has already computed. ⚠ A local is never resolved, and a false positive is the reason rather than cost. var iv = new byte[16]; RandomNumberGenerator.Fill(iv); aes.IV = iv; is how correct code is written, and a rule that followed iv to its declaration would report it — so the constant must be written at the assignment itself, or be the initialiser of a field holding an explicit list of literals. static readonly byte[] Iv = { 1, 2, … } is a hard-coded IV and cannot be anything else; = new byte[16] is the allocate-then-fill shape and is deliberately not followed. ⚠ Only the encrypting side. CreateDecryptor(key, iv) is handed the IV the message arrived with — that is what the overload is for, and reporting it would report the reader of a broken format rather than its writer. ⚠ Test methods are exempt, by the attribute test five other rules already use: a NIST or RFC test vector pins the IV by definition, and a security rule at error that breaks a crypto library's test suite is how a reviewer learns to skim past every security finding the tool makes. ⚠ The reference trees prove nothing here and the zero is reported as such: not one of the 4 459 files under Testing/corpus mentions System.Security.Cryptography, so the corpus zero is shape absent rather than correctly declined. The measurement that decides this rule is Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Tests/corpus/, where every safe file is the same shape as its vulnerable twin with the vulnerability removed the way a reviewer would remove it.
